newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Dec 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Dec 12.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- LABOUR CASTS DOUBT ON 700 MILLION STG MILLENNIUM PLAN

Labour, as a result of its refusal to give an open-ended commitment to providing financial support for a celebration of the new millennium to take place in Greenwich, has raised doubts about the plans going ahead at all. Labour heritage spokesman Jack Cunningham has called into question both the business plan for the celebration and the overall viability of the project.
Private sponsors of the event have warned they will withdraw unless Labour commits itself to covering any cost over-runs.
-- BULLISH AIRTOURS HAILS 46 PER CENT PROFIT RISE

The UK's second-largest tour operator Airtours has reported an increase of 46 percent in pre-tax profits to 86.8 million stg for the year to the end of September. The company noted that the sector had recovered from the downturn experienced last year and predicted improving prospects for 1997. Net profit per Airtours passenger increased from 9 stg to 14 stg thanks to a rise in prices that accompanied a decline in overall market volume.
-- HANSON RULES OUT SALE OF EASTERN BEFORE DEMERGER

Conglomerate Hanson has dismissed speculation that it might divest itself of Eastern Group in advance of a planned five-way demerger of the company. The dismissal of the suggestions came as Hanson revealed financial details relating to Energy Group, of which Eastern is an element. The data revealed that Energy Group has assets of 6.6 billion stg and made profits of 446 million stg in the year to the end of September.
-- MARKETS FALLS AS INVESTORS TAKE END-OF-YEAR PROFITS

Stock markets across the world once more experienced volatility as profit-taking by investors pushed share values lower. Additional factors leading to a fall on many share markets included doubts about Japanese commitment to US bond markets as well as political uncertainty surrounding US relations with Iran. Markets were described as having become nervous in the wake of comments last week from the Federal Reserve's Alan Greenspan which were interpreted as being a criticism of current share values.
-- OFT MAY HARDEN PRICE-FIX CURBS

The Office of Fair Trading is reported to be considering a tightening of regulation governing links between retailers and manufacturers. In particular, attention will be given to exclusive deals entered into whereby manufacturers forbid retailers from stocking goods produced by rivals. It is felt that such vertical arrangements can work against the interests of competition. Such deals have been found to operate in the beer and soft drinks market and have been the subject of a report compiled by the Monopolies & Mergers Commission.
-- EMU STABILITY PACT DEAL ON THE CARDS

There is reported to be increasing optimism among EU leaders that the forthcoming Dublin summit will result in a last-minute deal being reached on a stability pact for countries taking part in the single currency. To date, division has been created between member states by the insistence on the part of Germany that any such accord be rigidly applied. This would result in participating countries that exceeded budget spending targets being subject to automatic heavy financial penalties.
-- PETROL PRICE WAR BLAMED FOR SPENDING FREEZE

A report from the Petrol Pump Manufacturers Association has noted oil companies have reduced capital spending by up to 50 percent to protect profit margins that are under pressure as a result of a long-running price war at the forecourts. According to suppliers of equipment to the petrol retailing industry, this price war has lasted longer than anyone had anticipated and had more far-reaching effects. Shell has confirmed that continuing price pressure could impact adversely on its investment program.
-- INVESTMENT 'AMONG WORST OF INDUSTRIALISED NATIONS'

A report by Oxford Economic Forecasting for the Machine Tool Technologies Association has singled out Britain's industrial investment record as among the worst among industrialised nations. The conclusions run counter to government claims that the country's record in this field is ahead of competitor nations. The latest report is particularly critical of spending in the field of research and development and has led to calls for incentives to be offered in order to encourage investment.
-- MOBILE PHONE RATES SET TO RISE

It is anticipated that the costs for calls made to One-2-One and Orange mobile phones from British Telecom's network could rise sharply from February of 1997. Talks between all three operators on the issue of charges are currently underway, and increases are expected in a move that will allow the mobile companies to fully recover the costs of calls originating from BT's system. It is not expected that the price of calls to BT phones or other mobile operators will be affected.
